days.context_before:
Today covers a LOT of ground — Paul's missionary journeys across the Roman Empire.

Between Acts 11 and Acts 13, the gospel has been spreading. Believers scattered to Antioch in Syria (the third largest city in the Roman Empire). There, for the first time, they were called CHRISTIANS (Acts 11:26). The Antioch church became the launching point for the great missionary expansion.

Today we sample four scenes from Paul's three missionary journeys (roughly AD 46-58):
  - **Acts 13:1-3** — the commissioning at Antioch
  - **Acts 14:8-20** — at Lystra, Paul heals a lame man, is mistaken for a god, then stoned
  - **Acts 16:6-15** — the gospel crosses into Europe via a vision of a Macedonian man
  - **Acts 17:16-31** — Paul preaches at the Areopagus in Athens

By the end of Paul's journeys, churches have been planted in Asia Minor, Greece, and beyond.
days.plain_english_simple:
Today: Paul's missionary journeys across the Roman Empire.

**The commissioning (Acts 13:1-3).** In ANTIOCH the church is praying and fasting. The Holy Spirit speaks: SET APART FOR ME BARNABAS AND SAUL. The church lays hands on them and sends them out. Paul's first missionary journey begins.

From now on, the text increasingly calls Saul by his Roman name PAUL.

**At Lystra: from gods to stones (Acts 14:8-20).** Paul heals a man lame from birth. The crowd thinks Paul and Barnabas are gods (Hermes and Zeus). The priest of Zeus brings oxen for sacrifice. Paul and Barnabas TEAR THEIR CLOTHES in horror: MEN, WE ARE JUST MEN LIKE YOU. TURN FROM THESE VAIN THINGS TO THE LIVING GOD.

They barely stop the sacrifice. Then opponents arrive from another city, turn the crowd against Paul, and STONE HIM. They drag him outside the city, thinking he is dead. But he gets up. He walks back in. The next day, he leaves for the next town. This is the pattern: worship one moment, stones the next. He keeps going.

**Into Europe (Acts 16:6-15).** The Spirit blocks Paul from going certain directions. Then Paul has a vision at night: A MAN OF MACEDONIA stands and begs: COME OVER TO MACEDONIA AND HELP US.

Paul sails across the Aegean Sea. He lands at Philippi in northern Greece. There is no synagogue, so he meets a group of women praying by a river. One of them is LYDIA — a businesswoman who deals in purple cloth, a God-fearer. The text says: THE LORD OPENED HER HEART. She and her household are baptized. She is the FIRST EUROPEAN CONVERT. The European church begins in a businesswoman's house.

**At Athens (Acts 17:16-31).** Paul reaches ATHENS — the intellectual capital of the ancient world. The city is FULL OF IDOLS. The Epicurean and Stoic philosophers take him to the AREOPAGUS to hear him.

Paul gives one of the most brilliant sermons in the New Testament. He starts where they are: I see you are very religious. I saw an altar TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. Let me tell you about him.

He proclaims:
  - The God who made everything
  - Does not live in temples built by hands
  - Made every nation from one man
  - Is not far from any of us (Paul even quotes Greek poets)
  - In the past God overlooked ignorance
  - But NOW he commands all people everywhere to REPENT
  - Because he has fixed a day on which he will JUDGE the world
  - Through a man he raised from the dead

When Paul mentions the RESURRECTION, some MOCK. Some say WE WILL HEAR YOU AGAIN. A few BELIEVE.

**What this means.** Paul's three journeys planted churches across the empire. The pattern:
  - SPIRIT-LED — the mission moves where the Spirit directs
  - CULTURALLY ENGAGED — Paul speaks to fishermen, businesswomen, philosophers, each on their own terms
  - POWER AND SUFFERING TOGETHER — he heals AND is stoned
  - RESURRECTION IS THE CLIMAX — whether speaking to Jews or Gentiles or philosophers, Paul preaches the empty tomb
  - PERSISTENT — despite opposition, persecution, beatings, and stonings, he keeps going
days.plain_english_standard:
Today's reading samples four key scenes from Paul's three missionary journeys, spanning roughly 12-13 years (AD 46-58) and establishing Christian communities across the Roman Empire.

**The commissioning (Acts 13:1-3).** The scene opens in ANTIOCH IN SYRIA — the third largest city in the empire. The church is multi-ethnic. Five named leaders are listed: Barnabas (Jewish from Cyprus), Simeon called Niger (likely African), Lucius of Cyrene (North African), Manaen (raised with Herod the tetrarch), and Saul (former Pharisee).

The diversity is striking. Jewish, African, royal connection — the leadership embodied the multi-ethnic kingdom of God.

The church is WORSHIPING and FASTING. The Holy Spirit speaks: SET APART FOR ME BARNABAS AND SAUL FOR THE WORK TO WHICH I HAVE CALLED THEM.

More fasting. Prayer. Laying on of hands. They SEND THEM OUT. The first organized Christian missionary expedition has begun.

Note: from this point in Acts, Saul is increasingly called PAUL (his Roman name). The shift signals his pivot to Gentile mission.

**At Lystra: from gods to stones (Acts 14:8-20).** Paul and Barnabas arrive at LYSTRA in modern Turkey. They preach in the public square. A man lame from birth is there. Paul sees that he has FAITH to be made well. Paul calls out: STAND UP ON YOUR FEET. The man LEAPS UP and walks.

The crowd's reaction is culturally specific. Local mythology held that Zeus and Hermes had once visited Lystra in human form and been refused hospitality. The crowd assumes the gods have come back. They identify Barnabas as ZEUS (the elder) and Paul as HERMES (the messenger, because he did the talking). The priest of Zeus brings OXEN AND WREATHS for sacrifices.

Paul and Barnabas TEAR THEIR CLOTHES — the Jewish gesture of horror at blasphemy. They rush into the crowd: MEN, WHY ARE YOU DOING THESE THINGS? WE ARE MEN, OF THE SAME NATURE AS YOU. We bring you good news — TURN FROM THESE WORTHLESS THINGS TO THE LIVING GOD who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them.

Paul's short sermon (14:15-17) is one of the New Testament's clearest treatments of GENERAL REVELATION — God's witness to all peoples through creation and providence. Even pagans have evidence of God's existence in rain, harvest, food, joy.

They barely stop the sacrifice. Then Jewish opponents arrive from earlier cities and turn the crowd against Paul. The same crowd that wanted to sacrifice TO him now STONES HIM. They drag his body outside the city, thinking he is dead.

But he is not dead. The disciples gather around him. He gets up. He walks back into the city. The next day he leaves with Barnabas. (2 Corinthians 11:25 — 'once I was stoned' — likely refers to this.)

Worship to stones in one afternoon. He keeps going.

**Crossing into Europe (Acts 16:6-15).** On Paul's second journey, a divine redirect happens. The Holy Spirit FORBIDS Paul from preaching in some regions of Asia. The Spirit forbids him from going into Bithynia. Paul keeps trying directions. The Spirit keeps closing doors.

Finally at TROAS (on the western coast of Asia Minor), Paul has a VISION at night. A MAN OF MACEDONIA begs: COME OVER TO MACEDONIA AND HELP US.

Macedonia was across the Aegean Sea — in EUROPE. The gospel was about to cross a major geographic boundary.

Paul, Silas, Timothy, and Luke himself (note the shift to 'we' in 16:10, suggesting Luke joined the team here) sail across. They land at Philippi — a Roman colony in northern Greece.

There is no synagogue in Philippi. They go to a place outside the city by a river where Jewish women gather to pray. They sit down and talk with the women.

One of them is LYDIA:
  - From the city of THYATIRA (in Asia Minor, known for purple dye)
  - A SELLER OF PURPLE CLOTH — purple was the most expensive dye in the ancient world
  - A WORSHIPER OF GOD — a Gentile God-fearer

She is a businesswoman of means. She listens. The text adds the critical theological note: THE LORD OPENED HER HEART to pay attention to what was said by Paul.

This is a crucial sentence in Acts' theology of conversion. Lydia heard the gospel — but it was the LORD opening her heart that made the gospel effective. Conversion is the Lord's work.

Lydia and her household are baptized. The FIRST EUROPEAN CONVERT. She insists Paul's team stay at her house. The European church begins in the home of a businesswoman.

**At the Areopagus in Athens (Acts 17:16-31).** Paul reaches ATHENS — the intellectual capital of the ancient world. Centuries earlier this had been Socrates, Plato, Aristotle. By Paul's day, Athens was past its political peak but remained a center of philosophy.

Paul wanders the city and is GREATLY DISTRESSED. The Greek means 'provoked' or 'irritated.' The city is FULL OF IDOLS. Statues of gods, goddesses, and personifications everywhere.

Paul preaches in the synagogue, then in the AGORA (marketplace) — engaging anyone. Soon he attracts EPICUREAN and STOIC philosophers. They take him to the AREOPAGUS (Mars Hill, the philosophical court of Athens) to formally explain what he is preaching.

Paul's sermon at the Areopagus is one of the most brilliant in the New Testament. It is a model of cross-cultural communication:

**1. POINT OF CONTACT.** I see you are VERY RELIGIOUS. I observed an altar inscribed TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. I want to tell you about the God you worship in ignorance.

Paul has just turned Athenian religious instinct into a foothold for the gospel.

**2. CREATION.** The God who MADE THE WORLD AND EVERYTHING IN IT — Lord of heaven and earth — does not live in TEMPLES BUILT BY HUMAN HANDS. He gives life and breath to everything.

Paul is undermining the central religious practice of Athens.

**3. PROVIDENCE.** From ONE MAN he made every nation. He determined their times and places — SO THAT THEY MIGHT SEEK GOD. THOUGH HE IS NOT FAR FROM ANY ONE OF US.

**4. POETIC QUOTATION.** Paul quotes Greek poets: 'in him we live and move and have our being' (Epimenides) and 'we are also his offspring' (Aratus). He uses pagan literature to support biblical truth.

**5. THE TURN.** SINCE we are God's offspring, we should not think the deity is like GOLD OR SILVER OR STONE shaped by human craft.

In one move, Paul has dismantled the philosophical justification for the idols all around them.

**6. THE CLIMAX.** GOD OVERLOOKED THE TIMES OF IGNORANCE — but NOW HE COMMANDS ALL PEOPLE EVERYWHERE TO REPENT.

Because he has APPOINTED A DAY on which he will JUDGE the world in righteousness by THE MAN HE HAS APPOINTED. And he has given assurance to all by RAISING HIM FROM THE DEAD.

Paul never names Jesus directly in the Areopagus sermon. But he proclaims his resurrection.

**The response.** Three responses:
  - Some MOCK (the resurrection of the body was philosophically absurd to many Greeks)
  - Some say WE WILL HEAR YOU AGAIN (polite delay)
  - Some BELIEVE — including Dionysius the Areopagite (a member of the court — a high-status convert) and a woman named Damaris

The Athenian church started small. But it started.

**Why this matters.** Paul's missionary journeys planted churches across the empire. Each scene shows a different facet of his ministry:
  - **Spirit-led commissioning** (Antioch) — the mission begins where the Spirit speaks
  - **Miracles met with both worship and stones** (Lystra) — power and persecution come together
  - **Geographic breakthrough** (Philippi) — the gospel crosses into Europe via a businesswoman
  - **Intellectual engagement** (Athens) — the gospel can address the most sophisticated cultures

The shape of Paul's ministry has shaped Christian mission ever since: Spirit-led, culturally engaged, gospel-centered, willing to suffer, focused on the resurrection of Christ.
days.plain_english_deeper:
Paul's missionary journeys are the central narrative of the second half of Acts. Each of today's scenes carries theological depth.

**The Antioch commissioning model.** The pattern of Acts 13:1-3 has shaped Christian mission for 2,000 years:
  - A diverse leadership team
  - Communal worship and fasting (the church together is where God speaks)
  - Spirit-directed sending (not a strategic plan, but a Spirit-prompted call)
  - Confirmation by the community (the church laid hands and sent them)
  - Continued accountability (Paul and Barnabas returned to Antioch and reported back — Acts 14:27)

This is the apostolic missionary model. The church is the sending agency. The Spirit identifies and calls. The community confirms. Lone-ranger mission disconnected from a sending church is not the apostolic pattern.

**The Lystra incident as a study in general revelation.** Paul's response to being mistaken for a god is theologically rich. His sermon in Acts 14:15-17 has been called one of the clearest treatments of NATURAL THEOLOGY in the New Testament. Key claims:
  - The pagans' gods are VAIN/WORTHLESS
  - There is a LIVING GOD who made everything
  - In past generations, God allowed the nations to walk in their own ways
  - But God did not leave himself without witness — RAIN, FRUITFUL SEASONS, FOOD, GLADNESS

Paul is saying: even pagans have evidence of God's existence and goodness. The created order itself testifies. Romans 1:18-21 develops this further. Pagans are not 'innocent' in their idolatry — they have witnesses they have rejected. But God's grace has also been present even to pagans — through providence, beauty, joy.

This was Paul's strategy at both Lystra and Athens. He didn't start with the Hebrew Scriptures. He started with creation, providence, and the universal human longing for God.

**The stoning at Lystra.** Paul refers to his stoning later. 2 Corinthians 11:25 — 'once I was stoned.' 2 Timothy 3:11 — 'persecutions, sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra.' Paul does not stop. He gets up. He walks back into the city. The next day he leaves with Barnabas.

Later Paul will say (2 Corinthians 4:7-12): 'we are pressed on every side, yet not crushed; perplexed, yet not in despair; pursued, yet not forsaken; struck down, yet not destroyed.' The stoning at Lystra is the lived experience behind that theology.

**The Macedonian call.** Acts 16:9-10 records the vision. This brief account marks one of the most consequential geographic moments in church history. The shift from Paul-and-his-companions to 'WE' in the narrative (16:10) suggests that LUKE joined the team at Troas. He becomes an eyewitness.

The Spirit DIRECTS where mission goes. Paul had wanted to go elsewhere. The Spirit redirected. Europe specifically would become a cradle of subsequent Christian history.

**Lydia and divine initiative in conversion.** Lydia's conversion is theologically important. The text says THE LORD OPENED HER HEART. This is one of the clearest statements in Acts about the divine initiative in conversion. The proclamation is human. The opening of the heart is divine.

Calvinist theology has emphasized God's sovereign role in conversion based partly on texts like this. Arminian theology has emphasized human response. The text seems to hold both: Lydia heard, but the Lord opened her heart so that she heard rightly. Both human responsibility and divine initiative are present.

**Paul's Areopagus speech as a model of contextual preaching.** Paul's sermon in Athens has been studied for centuries. Several principles:
  - Start where the audience is
  - Affirm what can be affirmed
  - Use the audience's own sources
  - Lead from common ground to confrontation
  - Don't soften the central claim

Paul moved from creation (acceptable to Athenians) to providence to natural longing for God to the rejection of idolatry to the resurrection of Christ. He used cultural resources without compromising biblical content.

This model has shaped Christian preaching, missions, and apologetics ever since. Effective gospel communication starts where the audience is and leads them to Christ.

**For the reader.** Three notes.

First, the church grows by GOING. Paul didn't stay in Antioch and wait. The early church planted thousands of communities by sending missionaries. Wherever the church has been faithful to its missionary calling, it has spread.

Second, every missionary scene includes both POWER and SUFFERING. Paul healed the lame. Paul was stoned. The combination is not a contradiction. It is the pattern of Christian ministry.

Third, Paul met every audience where they were. Fishermen, businesswomen, philosophers — Paul preached to all of them, in language they could understand. He never compromised the gospel. He never delivered the same canned sermon. Know your audience. Know the gospel. Bring them together.
days.key_insight: Paul went out from Antioch by the Spirit. Stoned at Lystra, called into Europe, preaching the UNKNOWN GOD at Athens — some mocked, some believed. The pattern of Christian mission was set.
days.reflection_prompt: Paul met every audience where they were — fishermen, businesswomen, philosophers — using language and references they understood. Who is in your life that you have not been bringing the gospel to because you don't know how to talk with them?
days.application_action: Today, identify ONE person from a different background than you — different culture, education, profession, political view. Spend 10 minutes learning something they value. Use that as a possible bridge for relationship and witness.

confusion_topics.topic: Why did the Holy Spirit forbid Paul from preaching in some places?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Acts 16:6-7 records the Spirit forbidding Paul from preaching in Asia and Bithynia. The gospel IS for everyone — but the TIMING and SEQUENCE is in the Spirit's hands. The Spirit was directing Paul to Macedonia first. Asia would receive the gospel later — Paul would minister in Ephesus for years during his third journey. The principle: God has timing for every people group. We make plans. We are open to redirection. Closed doors are sometimes God's way of opening different doors.

confusion_topics.topic: Why did Paul quote pagan Greek poets in his Areopagus sermon?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Paul quoted Epimenides ('in him we live and move and have our being') and Aratus ('we are his offspring'). Strategic: Paul knew his audience. The philosophers would respect their own poets. Theologically: Paul recognized GENERAL REVELATION. Even pagan poets sometimes glimpse aspects of truth. Romans 1:19-20 says God's invisible attributes have been clearly seen. Pagans don't have ZERO truth. Paul affirmed truths he could (we ARE God's offspring) while challenging errors (so we should not think God can be sculpted in stone). The pattern continues: we can affirm whatever is true, good, and beautiful in any culture, leading such affirmations to Christ. We don't reject everything pagan; we don't accept everything pagan. We discern.

confusion_topics.topic: Were Paul and Barnabas the only missionaries?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: No — but Acts focuses on Paul because Luke (Acts's author) was Paul's traveling companion. According to Christian tradition, the twelve apostles spread out: Peter went to Rome; James was martyred early; John lived to old age in Ephesus; Thomas is traditionally believed to have gone to India; Andrew went to Scythia and Greece; Bartholomew possibly to Armenia and India; Matthew to Ethiopia; Philip to Asia Minor; Simon the Zealot to Persia; Jude to Mesopotamia. Most traditions hold that all twelve died as martyrs (except John). By AD 100, the gospel had reached most major Roman cities, the Persian Empire, parts of Africa, and possibly India.

confusion_topics.topic: What happened in cities where 'few believed'? Was Paul's ministry there a failure?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: By modern church-growth metrics, some of Paul's stops looked like failures. Athens produced only a handful of converts. But Paul's understanding of success was different. (1) FAITHFULNESS, NOT NUMBERS. Paul's job was to preach faithfully. The response was the Spirit's job. (2) SMALL BEGINNINGS, LONG RESULTS. The Athens church grew over time. (3) THE KINGDOM IS LARGER THAN THE VISIBLE. Many seeds grow years later. (4) PAUL HIMSELF NEVER SEEMED DISCOURAGED BY 'SMALL' RESULTS. He kept preaching, kept moving, kept planting. This is a corrective for contemporary Christianity, which often measures faithfulness by attendance and growth statistics. Paul measured faithfulness by faithfulness to the gospel. The numbers were the Lord's responsibility.

days.retention_anchor: Today Paul was sent out from Antioch by the Spirit's call. At Lystra they tried to worship him as a god, then stoned him. He got up and kept going. A vision called him into Europe — the first European convert was LYDIA, a businesswoman whose heart the Lord OPENED. At Athens he preached to philosophers about the UNKNOWN GOD and the resurrection. Tomorrow you see Paul reach Rome — in chains, fulfilling Jesus's commission to be his witness to the ends of the earth.

days.context_before:
Today closes Arc 10. Paul reaches ROME.

Between Acts 17 (Athens) and Acts 27 (the journey to Rome), much has happened. Paul ministered in CORINTH for 18 months, planting one of the most important early churches. He spent THREE YEARS in EPHESUS, working in the main city of Asia, where so many people came to faith that the silver-shrine sellers rioted (because their idol business was collapsing). He took up a collection from Gentile churches for the impoverished Jerusalem church — a powerful symbol of the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers.

Then Paul went to JERUSALEM. He was arrested. He was nearly killed by a mob. The Romans took him into protective custody. He was tried before the Sanhedrin, then before the Roman governor Felix, then before Felix's successor Festus, then before King Herod Agrippa II. Eventually, Paul (as a Roman citizen) APPEALED TO CAESAR — invoking his right to be tried before the Emperor in Rome.

The Romans had to send him. Acts 27 narrates the SHIPWRECK on the journey. Today's reading covers two scenes from that journey:

  - **Acts 27:13-26** — the storm at sea. An angel appears to Paul during the storm. He encourages the 276 people aboard the ship. He prophesies that the ship will be lost but everyone will survive.
  - **Acts 28:11-31** — Paul arrives in Rome. Believers come to meet him. He spends two years under house arrest, freely preaching the kingdom of God.

Acts ends here. Not with Paul's martyrdom. Not with a great triumph. With Paul in Rome, in his own rented house, preaching openly and without hindrance. The gospel has reached the heart of the empire.
days.plain_english_simple:
Today closes Arc 10. Paul reaches ROME.

Between Acts 17 and Acts 27, Paul:
  - Spent 18 months in CORINTH planting a church
  - Spent 3 years in EPHESUS, where so many converted the silver-idol industry collapsed
  - Took up a Gentile-church collection for the poor Jerusalem church
  - Returned to Jerusalem and was ARRESTED
  - Was tried before the Sanhedrin, Roman governors Felix and Festus, and King Agrippa
  - Finally, as a ROMAN CITIZEN, APPEALED TO CAESAR — invoking his right to trial before the Emperor

The Romans had to send him to Rome. Today: the journey there.

**The shipwreck (Acts 27).** Paul is a prisoner on a Roman grain ship sailing from the eastern Mediterranean toward Italy. There are 276 people on board.

It is late in the sailing season. A storm hits — a EUROCLYDON, a northeast wind. The ship is driven for days. Sun and stars are not visible. The crew throws cargo overboard to lighten the ship. After many days, all hope is lost. The text says: ALL HOPE THAT WE WOULD BE SAVED WAS NOW TAKEN AWAY.

Then Paul stands up among them. He had warned them not to sail this late, but they hadn't listened. Now he speaks to encourage them:

LAST NIGHT AN ANGEL OF THE GOD TO WHOM I BELONG AND WHOM I SERVE STOOD BY ME. THE ANGEL SAID: DON'T BE AFRAID, PAUL. YOU MUST STAND BEFORE CAESAR. AND BEHOLD — GOD HAS GRANTED YOU THE LIVES OF ALL WHO SAIL WITH YOU.

Then: SO TAKE COURAGE, MEN. I BELIEVE GOD. IT WILL HAPPEN JUST AS HE TOLD ME.

The ship breaks apart on a beach at MALTA (an island south of Italy). All 276 people make it to shore. Not one is lost. Paul's prophecy was exactly fulfilled.

On Malta, Paul ministers to the locals for three months. He heals many people. The Maltese show them great kindness. Then, when sailing resumes, they take ship for Italy.

**Reaching Rome (Acts 28).** They land at PUTEOLI (near modern Naples) and find Christian believers there. The believers in Rome have heard Paul is coming. Some of them travel about 40 miles south to meet him on the road — at a place called the Forum of Appius. Others meet him at the Three Taverns (about 30 miles from Rome).

The text records a touching moment: WHEN PAUL SAW THEM, HE THANKED GOD AND TOOK COURAGE.

Paul has wanted to come to Rome for years. He wrote his letter to the Romans long before he ever got there. Now he is finally arriving — in chains, as a prisoner. But the brothers come to meet him. He sees them. He thanks God. He takes courage.

In Rome, Paul is allowed to live in his own rented house with one Roman soldier as his guard. He is technically under house arrest, but he is free to receive visitors.

Within three days, he calls together the leaders of the Roman Jewish community. He tells them his story. He spends a full day preaching to them about Jesus — from the Law of Moses AND from the prophets — from morning until evening.

Some believe. Others reject. The pattern is consistent.

**The closing scene (Acts 28:30-31).** Acts ends with one of the most striking closing scenes in any book of the Bible:

PAUL STAYED TWO WHOLE YEARS IN HIS OWN RENTED HOUSE. HE WELCOMED ALL WHO CAME TO HIM. HE PREACHED THE KINGDOM OF GOD AND TAUGHT ABOUT THE LORD JESUS CHRIST WITH ALL BOLDNESS, WITHOUT HINDRANCE.

That is how Acts ends.

Notice what it does NOT say. It does NOT say what happened to Paul after the two years. It does NOT describe his trial before Nero. It does NOT mention his eventual martyrdom (which church tradition holds happened under Nero around AD 67).

Luke deliberately ends with Paul in Rome, preaching freely. The geographic commission of Acts 1:8 — 'you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth' — has been fulfilled. The gospel has reached Rome, the heart of the empire. From Rome, it will continue spreading. The story is not over. But the foundational chapter is complete.

**What this means.** Arc 10 closes with the gospel established in Rome. From here, the church will continue spreading throughout the empire and beyond.

Within a few centuries:
  - Christianity will spread across the entire Roman Empire
  - It will become the official religion (AD 380, under Theodosius)
  - It will continue spreading north into Europe, east to Persia and India, south into Africa
  - Eventually, by the modern era, it will reach every continent

All downstream from the events of Acts. All starting with 120 people in an upper room. All possible because of what Christ did at the cross and the empty tomb — and because of the Holy Spirit's empowering of ordinary people to be his witnesses to the ends of the earth.

Tomorrow you start Arc 11 — the LETTERS the apostles wrote to the churches they planted. Each letter is a window into the early church's questions, problems, and theology. Each letter still speaks to the church today.
days.plain_english_standard:
Today closes Arc 10. Paul reaches ROME — the heart of the Roman Empire, the symbolic 'ends of the earth' for a first-century audience.

**The arc from Athens to Rome.** Between Acts 17 (Athens) and Acts 28 (Rome), Paul has lived through years of intense ministry and suffering:

  - **Corinth (18 months)** — Paul planted the Corinthian church, where he made tents for his living, debated in the synagogue, was opposed by Jewish leaders, and brought many to faith. He wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians during this time.
  - **Ephesus (3 years)** — Paul's longest stay in any city. He worked daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus. So many converted that the silver-shrine sellers (who made replicas of Artemis's temple) rioted, fearing their business was collapsing. The riot was so intense Paul was nearly killed. He wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus.
  - **Macedonian return** — Paul revisited churches in Macedonia and Greece. He wrote 2 Corinthians, Galatians, and Romans during this period.
  - **Jerusalem collection** — Paul organized a massive collection from Gentile churches across the empire for the impoverished Jerusalem church. The collection was a powerful symbol of Jew-Gentile unity in Christ.
  - **Jerusalem arrest** — Paul went to Jerusalem with the collection. He was accused of bringing a Gentile into the temple courts (a false accusation). A mob nearly killed him. Roman soldiers rescued him.
  - **Two years in Caesarean prison** — Paul was held by Governor Felix for two years awaiting trial. Felix's successor Festus eventually tried him. King Agrippa II also heard his testimony.
  - **Appeal to Caesar** — As a Roman citizen, Paul invoked his right to be tried before the EMPEROR in Rome. The Romans had to send him.

This was around AD 59-60. Paul is now around 55-60 years old. He has been an apostle for about 25-30 years. He has planted churches across the empire. He is now headed to Rome — not as a triumphant missionary but as a chained prisoner.

**The shipwreck (Acts 27).** Acts 27 is one of the most detailed accounts of ancient seafaring in any surviving document. Luke describes the journey, the ships used, the ports of call, the wind directions, the maritime decisions — with the precision of an eyewitness.

Paul is a prisoner on a Roman grain ship carrying wheat from Alexandria (Egypt) to Italy. There are 276 people on board — passengers, crew, and prisoners. The ship is sailing late in the season (after the Day of Atonement, mid-October), when Mediterranean sailing was considered dangerous.

Paul WARNS the centurion (the Roman officer in charge of the prisoners) and the ship's captain not to continue. The captain disregards Paul's warning. They sail.

A storm hits — a EUROCLYDON, a violent northeast wind. The ship is driven for many days. Sun and stars are not visible. The crew throws CARGO and TACKLE overboard to lighten the ship. After many days, the text says: ALL HOPE THAT WE WOULD BE SAVED WAS NOW TAKEN AWAY.

Then Paul stands up among them (27:21-26). He gently mentions that they should have listened to him at first (27:21 — not as 'I told you so' but as a reminder that his judgment had been right). Then he gives them the message:

TAKE HEART. NO ONE WILL BE LOST. ONLY THE SHIP. LAST NIGHT AN ANGEL OF THE GOD TO WHOM I BELONG AND WHOM I SERVE STOOD BY ME, SAYING: DO NOT BE AFRAID, PAUL. YOU MUST STAND BEFORE CAESAR. AND BEHOLD — GOD HAS GRANTED YOU ALL THOSE WHO SAIL WITH YOU.

Then Paul's testimony: TAKE HEART, MEN. I BELIEVE GOD. IT WILL HAPPEN JUST AS HE TOLD ME.

The scene is remarkable. The prisoner is now the most stable person on the ship. The man supposedly being transported in chains is the one delivering hope to those nominally in charge.

The ship breaks apart on a beach at MALTA (an island south of Sicily). All 276 people make it to shore. Not one is lost. Paul's prophecy is exactly fulfilled.

On Malta, Paul is bitten by a viper while gathering firewood. The Maltese expect him to die. He doesn't. They then expect him to be a god (the same pattern as Lystra). He just keeps ministering. He heals the father of Publius (the chief official of the island) and many others. They stay three months.

**Arriving in Rome (Acts 28:11-16).** When the sailing season opens in spring, they board another Alexandrian grain ship. They sail to Syracuse (Sicily), then Rhegium (mainland Italy), then PUTEOLI (near modern Naples) — about 150 miles south of Rome.

At Puteoli, they find Christian believers and stay with them seven days. The Roman authorities allow this — Paul has been a model prisoner, and the centurion (whose life Paul has just saved) is treating him generously.

Word reaches the Roman church that Paul is coming. The Roman Christians (whom Paul had written to years earlier but never met in person) travel south to meet him. Some come 40 miles to the FORUM OF APPIUS. Others come 30 miles to the THREE TAVERNS (a rest stop on the Appian Way).

The text records a touching moment (28:15): WHEN PAUL SAW THEM, HE THANKED GOD AND TOOK COURAGE.

This is one of the most human moments in Acts. Paul — apostle to the Gentiles, author of Romans, future martyr — needed to be encouraged. Seeing fellow Christians from the Roman church gave him courage. He had been imprisoned, shipwrecked, snake-bit, on the verge of death multiple times. The brotherhood of believers refreshed him.

This is the church doing what the church is supposed to do. Coming to meet the suffering, the imprisoned, the worn-out. Refreshing one another. Carrying one another's burdens.

In Rome, Paul is given a remarkable privilege. He is allowed to live in his own rented house with one Roman soldier as his guard (28:16). Technically house arrest. Practically, almost full freedom to live and minister.

**Paul's ministry in Rome (Acts 28:17-29).** Within three days of his arrival, Paul calls together the leaders of the Roman Jewish community. He explains his story:

  - I was arrested in Jerusalem and turned over to the Romans
  - The Romans found nothing deserving of death and wanted to release me
  - When the Jews objected, I appealed to Caesar — not to accuse my own nation
  - I am here in chains BECAUSE OF THE HOPE OF ISRAEL — the hope of resurrection in Christ

The Roman Jews say they haven't heard anything bad about Paul from Judea. They want to hear his views. They appoint a day. Many people come.

Paul spends an ENTIRE DAY preaching — from morning until evening — TESTIFYING ABOUT THE KINGDOM OF GOD and PERSUADING THEM ABOUT JESUS from the LAW OF MOSES and the PROPHETS.

Some believe. Others don't. Paul quotes Isaiah 6:9-10 — the same passage Jesus had applied to spiritually hardened hearts — about ears that hear but don't understand, eyes that see but don't perceive.

Then Paul makes the formal pivot (28:28): THIS SALVATION OF GOD HAS BEEN SENT TO THE GENTILES. THEY WILL LISTEN.

The Roman Jews who reject the message leave. Paul continues his ministry to whoever will come.

**The closing scene (Acts 28:30-31).** The book of Acts ends with what may be the most theologically pregnant closing scene in any biblical book:

PAUL STAYED TWO WHOLE YEARS IN HIS OWN RENTED HOUSE. HE WELCOMED ALL WHO CAME TO HIM, PREACHING THE KINGDOM OF GOD AND TEACHING ABOUT THE LORD JESUS CHRIST WITH ALL BOLDNESS, WITHOUT HINDRANCE.

The Greek word for 'without hindrance' is *akōlytōs* — the last word of the book of Acts. The very last word.

Notice what the closing does NOT include:

  - It does NOT describe Paul's trial before Nero
  - It does NOT mention his outcome
  - It does NOT record his eventual martyrdom (church tradition holds he was beheaded by Nero around AD 67)
  - It does NOT bring closure to Paul's story

Why does Luke end this way? Several reasons:

  - **The book is about THE GOSPEL, not about Paul.** Acts is the story of how the gospel reached from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. Paul is the central human character of the second half, but he is not the point. The gospel is the point. The gospel has reached Rome. The story Luke set out to tell is complete.
  - **The point is UNHINDERED preaching.** Despite Paul being a prisoner, despite all the persecution, despite the storms (literal and metaphorical), the gospel is being proclaimed FREELY and BOLDLY in the heart of the Roman Empire. The mission Jesus commissioned in Acts 1:8 has been fulfilled.
  - **The story CONTINUES.** Luke ends without closure because the story doesn't end. Acts 29 is the church across history — the ongoing story of the gospel reaching the ends of the earth. Every Christian who has ever proclaimed Christ since AD 62 has been continuing the unfinished story.

Not Paul's death. Not a great triumph. The gospel being preached freely, by an apostle in chains, in the heart of the empire — that is where Luke chooses to end.

**Why this matters.** Arc 10 closes with the gospel established in Rome. From here, the church will continue spreading throughout the empire and beyond.

Within a few centuries:
  - Christianity will spread across the entire Roman Empire
  - The Edict of Milan (AD 313, under Constantine) will give it legal recognition
  - The Council of Nicaea (AD 325) will formalize key doctrines
  - Theodosius (AD 380) will make it the official religion of the empire
  - It will spread north into Europe, east to Persia and India, south into Africa
  - Eventually, by the modern era, it will reach every continent

All downstream from the events of Acts. All starting with 120 people in an upper room. All possible because of what Christ did at the cross and the empty tomb — and because of the Holy Spirit's empowering of ordinary people to be his witnesses to the ends of the earth.

Tomorrow you start Arc 11 — the LETTERS the apostles wrote to the churches they planted. Each letter is a window into the early church's questions, problems, and theology. Each letter still speaks to the church today.
days.plain_english_deeper:
Acts ends with one of the most theologically loaded closing scenes in the New Testament. Several deeper layers warrant attention.

**The voyage as a literary set-piece.** Acts 27 is famous in the history of literature as one of the most detailed seafaring narratives in any ancient document. Luke (a careful historian) records:

  - Specific ports (Caesarea, Sidon, Myra, Crete, Cauda, Malta, Syracuse, Rhegium, Puteoli)
  - Wind directions and ship maneuvering decisions
  - The Euroclydon storm and the technical sailing responses
  - The crew's actions (throwing cargo, jettisoning tackle, taking soundings)
  - The breaking of the ship on the beach

Scholars have used this account to study first-century maritime practice. The technical details are remarkably accurate. This is the kind of writing that comes from an eyewitness who paid attention.

Luke joins Paul on this voyage (the 'we' passages return in Acts 27). He was there. He recorded what he saw.

**Paul as the prisoner who saves everyone.** The narrative arc of Acts 27 is theologically striking. Paul is the LOWEST-status person on the ship. He is a prisoner. He has no legal authority. The centurion, the captain, the ship's owner — all outrank him.

Yet Paul becomes the SAVIOR of the ship in three ways:

  - He WARNS them not to sail (they should have listened)
  - He ENCOURAGES them during the storm with his vision and prophecy
  - He KEEPS the soldiers from killing the prisoners when the ship breaks up (27:42-43 — the soldiers wanted to kill all the prisoners so none would escape; the centurion stopped them to save Paul, which saved them all)

The pattern is theologically loaded. The prisoner saves the warden. The bound saves the free. The man in chains is the man with the inside line to God. This is the upside-down kingdom of Christ in narrative form.

Luke is making a point about Paul (and by extension, Christian witness). The world's hierarchies don't determine actual influence. The prisoner in the storm may be the one God has appointed to save the lives of everyone aboard.

**The Roman Christians' welcome.** The detail in Acts 28:15 — that Paul saw the brothers from Rome and TOOK COURAGE — is one of the most touching moments in Acts.

Paul had written his letter to the Romans years before he had ever visited Rome. The Roman church had heard about Paul. They had been praying for him. Now he arrives — chained, exhausted, recovering from shipwreck and snake-bite. Some of them travel up to 40 miles to meet him on the road.

The encouragement Paul received was real. Even apostles need encouragement. Even spiritual giants face exhaustion and discouragement. Paul thanked God and took courage. This is the church doing what the church is supposed to do.

This has implications for Christian community today. We are called to be the ones who come to meet the worn-out, the suffering, the imprisoned. Hebrews 10:24 — 'consider how to provoke one another to love and good works.' Hebrews 13:3 — 'remember those who are in bonds, as bound with them.' Paul felt this in the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. We extend it to others now.

**The kingdom of God as Paul's central message.** Acts 28:23 and 28:31 both name Paul's central message: THE KINGDOM OF GOD. This is interesting because Paul's letters more often focus on JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH, RECONCILIATION, ADOPTION, UNION WITH CHRIST — themes that frame the kingdom in particular ways.

But Acts is clear: Paul's preached message was THE KINGDOM. The kingdom message included:
  - The fulfillment of Old Testament hope (the king has come)
  - The lordship of Christ
  - The forgiveness of sins
  - The call to repentance and faith
  - The expectation of Christ's return
  - The ethical demands of kingdom life

Paul's letters develop specific aspects of kingdom life for specific church situations. His sermons proclaimed the kingdom itself. The two are not in tension; they are complementary.

This suggests that contemporary preaching should hold both — the proclamation of the kingdom (Christ's reign breaking in) AND the development of its implications (justification, sanctification, ethics, community life). One without the other is incomplete.

**The ending of Acts as theological statement.** Why does Luke end Acts without resolving Paul's trial outcome? Several possibilities, probably all operating:

  - **The story is about the gospel, not Paul.** Acts 1:8 set the goal — witnesses to the ends of the earth. Rome was effectively the ends of the earth. Once the gospel was there, the story Luke set out to tell was complete.
  - **The point is unhindered preaching.** The word *akōlytōs* (without hindrance) is the final word. Paul is in chains. The gospel is not.
  - **The story continues.** The church will keep spreading. Acts is not a closed book; it's an open call.
  - **Luke may have been writing before Paul's death.** Some scholars hold that Acts was written around AD 62, before Paul's eventual martyrdom in AD 67. If so, Luke ends with what he knew at the time.
  - **Paul's death is not the point.** Whether Paul lived two more years or twenty, the gospel had reached Rome. The mission had been accomplished. Paul's individual destiny was secondary to the message's spread.

Whatever the reason, the ending is theologically powerful. The book that began with Jesus's commission to take the gospel to the ends of the earth ends with the gospel in the heart of the empire, being preached without hindrance. The story Luke set out to tell is complete.

**Paul's prison letters and his death.** Although Acts ends here, we know more about Paul's life from his letters and church tradition:

  - During this two-year Roman imprisonment, Paul wrote EPHESIANS, PHILIPPIANS, COLOSSIANS, and PHILEMON — the 'prison epistles.'
  - Tradition holds that Paul was RELEASED after his first Roman imprisonment (around AD 62) and possibly ministered further — perhaps even reaching Spain (Romans 15:24 had mentioned this hope).
  - He was later RE-ARRESTED. The PASTORAL EPISTLES (1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus) may date from this period.
  - He was eventually EXECUTED by Nero — beheaded (a Roman citizen's privilege, sparing him crucifixion), probably around AD 67-68.

2 Timothy is traditionally read as Paul's last letter, written from his second Roman imprisonment shortly before his execution. The closing words (2 Timothy 4:6-8) are striking: 'For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith. From now on, there is stored up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give to me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all those who have loved his appearing.'

This is how Paul faced his death. Not as defeat. As a finished race. The man who began as Saul the persecutor ended as Paul the martyr — having brought the gospel to the ends of the earth.

**For the reader.** Three notes.

First, the gospel reached Rome through a PRISONER. Paul came in chains. He had been beaten, shipwrecked, snake-bit, on the verge of death multiple times. His ministry didn't look successful by most external measures. He had every reason to despair. And yet he kept preaching. The gospel reached the heart of the empire through a man who had every excuse to give up.

Second, the community matters. Paul TOOK COURAGE when the Roman brothers came to meet him. Even apostles need encouragement. We are called to be the kind of believers who travel to meet the worn-out, the imprisoned, the suffering. Don't underestimate what your presence might mean to a tired Christian.

Third, the book is unfinished BECAUSE THE STORY IS UNFINISHED. Acts 29 is the church across history — every Christian generation continuing what the apostles began. The gospel still spreads. The mission still continues. The unhindered preaching of Paul's house in Rome continues in every faithful gospel-speaking community in the world today. You and I are part of Acts. The story keeps going.
days.key_insight: Paul reached Rome in chains and preached two years FREELY, WITHOUT HINDRANCE. Acts ends with the gospel in the empire — Acts 1:8 fulfilled. The story continues in every generation since.

confusion_topics.topic: What happened to Paul after Acts ends? Did he die in Rome?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Acts ends in approximately AD 62 with Paul under house arrest in Rome, freely preaching for two years. Acts does not tell us what happened next. Tradition and Paul's letters fill in the picture. (1) Paul was likely RELEASED after his first Roman imprisonment. The Roman charges seem to have collapsed, and the case was either dismissed or decided in his favor. (2) He may have ministered further. Romans 15:24 mentions his hope to reach Spain. Some early Christian sources (Clement of Rome around AD 96) suggest he did reach Spain. (3) The PASTORAL EPISTLES (1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus) suggest further ministry in Ephesus, Crete, and Macedonia. (4) He was RE-ARRESTED, probably around AD 66-67, during Nero's persecution after the great fire of Rome. (5) He was EXECUTED — beheaded (a Roman citizen's privilege, sparing him crucifixion), probably around AD 67-68. 2 Timothy is traditionally read as his last letter, written shortly before his execution. His final words there: 'I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith' (2 Timothy 4:7). Tradition places his burial site at what is now St. Paul Outside the Walls in Rome. He died as he had lived — bearing witness to Christ.

confusion_topics.topic: Why does Acts end without telling us what happened? Isn't that strange?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: It IS unusual — and it is one of the most discussed features of Acts. Several theories: (1) LUKE WROTE BEFORE PAUL'S DEATH. Acts may have been written around AD 62, during Paul's first Roman imprisonment. If so, Luke didn't know what happened next because it hadn't happened yet. (2) THE BOOK IS ABOUT THE GOSPEL, NOT PAUL. Acts 1:8 set the goal — witnesses to the ends of the earth. Rome was effectively the ends of the earth. Once the gospel was there, the story Luke set out to tell was complete. Paul's individual fate is secondary. (3) THE POINT IS UNHINDERED PREACHING. The Greek word *akōlytōs* (without hindrance) is the very last word of Acts. Paul is in chains; the gospel is not. (4) THE STORY CONTINUES. Luke deliberately leaves Acts open-ended because the church's mission is ongoing. Every Christian generation since has been continuing 'Acts 29.' Whatever the reason, the ending is theologically powerful. The mission has reached Rome. The gospel is being preached freely. The story keeps going.

confusion_topics.topic: Did Paul really survive a snake bite on Malta? Doesn't that sound legendary?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Acts 28:3-6 records that a viper fastened on Paul's hand while he was gathering firewood. The natives expected him to die. He didn't. There are several reasonable readings: (1) IT WAS GENUINELY MIRACULOUS. God protected Paul because his commission to stand before Caesar required him to survive. Jesus had also promised in Mark 16:18 that some believers would 'take up serpents' without harm. (2) THE SNAKE'S BITE MAY NOT HAVE BEEN VENOMOUS. Some scholars note that no venomous vipers are currently native to Malta. The species may have been driven extinct, or the snake may have been a non-venomous look-alike. (3) PAUL'S RAPID SHAKING OFF OF THE SNAKE MAY HAVE PREVENTED FULL ENVENOMATION. Even venomous snakes sometimes give 'dry bites' without injecting venom. Whichever reading is right, the text emphasizes the LOCALS' interpretation — they expected him to die. He didn't. They concluded he must be a god. Paul kept ministering. The same pattern as Lystra — Paul refusing to be worshiped but using the moment to point to Christ.

confusion_topics.topic: Why didn't God just rescue Paul instead of letting him die under Nero?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: This is one of the recurring questions in Christian life. Several considerations. (1) GOD'S PURPOSES were larger than Paul's individual survival. Paul's death capped a faithful life that had planted churches across the empire. His martyrdom became one more witness. His prison letters (Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Philemon, the Pastorals) became Scripture. The world received treasures from Paul's imprisonment that it would not have received from his comfortable retirement. (2) GOD HAD ALREADY KEPT HIM ALIVE for the mission. Paul survived stoning, shipwreck, snakebite, multiple imprisonments, beatings. God preserved him until his mission was complete — then released him to glory. (3) DEATH IS NOT THE WORST THING. Paul himself wrote (Philippians 1:23): 'to depart and be with Christ is far better.' For Paul, dying was gain. The execution was the door to the presence of Christ he had loved and proclaimed. (4) MARTYRDOM IS WITNESS. The Greek for 'martyr' (*martys*) means 'witness.' Paul's death was his final witness to Christ. He died as he had lived — bearing testimony. The same questions apply to every believer's suffering and eventual death. God's purposes are larger than we can see. Death is not the end. Faithfulness through suffering and death is the highest form of witness. Paul's life embodied all of this.

days.retention_anchor: Today closed Arc 10. Paul reached ROME — in chains, as a prisoner. On the way, he saved 276 people from a shipwreck. In Rome, brothers traveled 40 miles to meet him; he THANKED GOD AND TOOK COURAGE. For two whole years he preached the kingdom of God and taught about Jesus FREELY, WITHOUT HINDRANCE. Acts ends with that one word — UNHINDERED. The gospel has reached the heart of the empire. Tomorrow Arc 11 begins — the LETTERS the apostles wrote to the churches they planted.
